core_insight: Speed at an instant makes sense as the value that average speeds over shorter and shorter intervals settle on - geometrically, the slope that secant lines approach as they pivot into the tangent.
prerequisites: slope of a straight line as rise over run
an informal idea of a limit
key_ideas: Average rate of change over an interval is the slope of a secant line.
Setting the interval to zero directly gives the meaningless 0/0.
Shrinking the interval makes the secant slopes approach one value; zoomed in, a smooth curve looks straight.
That limiting slope is the derivative: f'(x) = lim_{h->0} (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h.
Worked example: for x squared the difference quotient is 2x + h, so the derivative is 2x.
intuitions: A car's speedometer reading at one moment.
Zooming into a smooth curve until it looks like a straight line.
A secant line pivoting around a fixed point until it just touches the curve.
misconceptions: That the derivative is found by plugging h = 0 into the difference quotient (it gives 0/0).
That the tangent line must touch the curve at only one point.
That the derivative is a single number rather than a new function of x.
visual_opportunities: A dot moving along a road while its distance is measured.
A secant line through two points of a curve whose second point slides toward the first.
Live readouts of h and of the secant's slope converging.
A camera zoom into a point of the curve until it looks straight.
A tangent line sliding along a parabola with its slope read out as 2x.
